title: FAST '26 - Xerxes: Extensive Exploration of Scalable Hardware Systems with CXL-Based Simulation...
transcriptText:
Hello everyone. I'm Haoguo from Tsinghua
University. I'm presenting this work on
behalf of the authors from Peking
University and their collaborators.
This paper is titled Xerxes, extensive
exploration of scalable hardware systems
with CXL-based simulation framework.
First, let's look at the motivation. CXL
3 introduces features like port-based
routing and device managed coherence,
enabling arbitrary non-tree topologies
that go beyond the traditional
host-centric hierarchies in CPU memory
systems.
This is a conflict with traditional
research, which assumes a host-centric
system.
The problem is a simulation void. We
don't have CXL 3.0 hardware yet, and
existing simulators aren't good enough
to model these new fabric behaviors.
Xerxes is designed to fix this.
Specifically, there's a big gap between
protocol evolution and hardware
availability.
As you can see on the timeline, CXL 3
was defined in 2022, introducing major
features like back invalidation and
peer-to-peer topologies.
However, hardware is lagging. Even in
2024, full CXL 3 hardware is still
unavailable. Because of this, simulation
is the only viable path for research
right now. Looking deeper, CXL 1 started
in 2019 with basic expansion. CXL 2
added memory pooling in 2020, but
hardware for this has only partially
caught up.
This lag means researchers must simulate
to study advanced features like non-tree
topologies and distributed coherence.
So, why do existing tools fall short?
First, real hardware isn't commercially
available at scale, so we cannot test
complex rack-scale dynamics. Second,
traditional simulators typically fall
into two categories, computation-centric
and network-centric. Computation-centric
simulators, such as Gem5 and GP GPU-Sim,
are built around a host-centric
architectural model.
They model memory as a strict hierarchy
of components tightly coupled to CPU,
lacking a flexible interconnect layer
capable of modeling a scalable CXL
fabric.
Network-centric simulators, like BookSim
and Garnet, are designed to simulate
complex network topologies and routing
algorithms, but are fundamentally
unaware of memory and coherence
semantics, as they model generic packets
rather than stateful memory requests.
Third, NUMA emulation lacks physical
layer fidelity. It cannot model PCIe
behaviors like flow control and lane
contention.
In more detail, these flaws mean that
current methods cannot accurately
capture protocol interactions, such as
distributed nature of CXL coherence,
leading to unreliable results to
large-scale systems.
Xerxes was built to solve these specific
challenges.
Now, let's move to design of Xerxes.
Xerxes is a novel framework. It uses a
decoupled architecture and graph-based
connectivity to faithfully model CXL 3
mechanisms.
This design allows for a modular
simulation of diverse components,
ensuring scalability and accuracy in
representing emerging CXL features.
Here's the high-level architecture. We
separate the system into two layers to
make it scalable. The device layer in
blue models components like hosts and
accelerators as independent components.
The interconnect layer in red manages
the connections. It uses a graph-based
approach to support arbitrary topologies
using port-based routing.
We also provide extensible interfaces to
easily attach existing simulators like
DRAMSim3.
This two-layer approach decouples
physical connectivity from device logic,
enabling simulation of complex
non-hierarchical fabrics that
traditional tools cannot handle.
Let's look closer at the device layer.
It features like a modular component
design, like devices like hosts,
expanders, or endpoints are modeled as
isolated blocks.
This supports plug-and-play. Users can
add the new devices without changing the
existing code. It is also highly
extensible for developers to create
custom CXL devices.
Devices act as a peer independent
components, managing their own state,
which aligns with CXL's shift away from
host-centric models.
Next is the interconnect layer.
This layer models the topology as a
graph, where devices are nodes and
connections are edges. Crucially, it
natively supports port-based routing.
This allows us to simulate non-tree
fabric, which is a key feature of CXL 3.
Configuration is simple, making it easy
to define complex scalable fabrics.
Port-based routing enables flexible
forwarding, supporting arbitrary
topologies via routing tables, which is
essential for rack-scale systems.
Now, let's detail the key components.
The requester models the computation. It
acts as the source of memory request,
simulating a CPU or accelerator. It has
two modes, a request generator for
synthetic workloads and trace replay for
running real-world traces.
Internally, it handles queuing, address
translation, and caching before requests
enter the fabric.
This component ensures accurate modeling
of more memory request origins,
including address mapping and the
coherence management at the source.
For the interconnect, we have the bus
and the switch. The bus connects two
devices. It models PCIe 5 or 6 links,
supporting full duplex bandwidth
allocation.
The switch supports port-based routing.
Each port has configurable bandwidth,
and it supports custom routing policies,
allowing us to simulate diverse network
topologies.
These elements capture PCIe specific
behaviors like bidirectional links and
adaptive routing, critical for realistic
CXL simulation.
For coherence, Xerxes implements device
managed coherence.
This offloads coherence work from the
host to the devices.
Xerxes includes an inclusive snoop
filter. It tracks who shares the data.
If there's a conflict, the device
coherence agent issues a back invalid
snoops to peers, collects responses, and
grants ownership.
DMC enables scalable peer-to-peer
communication, reducing host overhead,
and the snoop filter's inclusive design
tracks sharers in device memory modes
modes like HDM-DB.
Xerxes is also extensible. For example,
we integrate it with DRAMSim3 for
accurate memory simulation. The
challenge is synchronizing the clocks.
The solution is a clocking event
mechanism that syncs the two simulation
domains.
This integration allows seamless
attachment of third-party models without
kernel modifications, enhancing
simulation fidelity.
The next part is simulator validation.
We calibrated Xerxes against real
hardware to ensure the results are
accurate and trustworthy.
This step is crucial to validate the
framework's predictive capabilities for
unreleased features.
The calibration platform uses a
fourth-generation Intel Xeon processor
and a Montage CXL memory expander.
We tuned simulator parameters like
arbitration delays and buffer sizes to
match the measurements from these
physical hardware.
This establishes a solid ground truth
baseline.
The methodology involved empirical
measurements of latency and bandwidth to
align simulation with real CXL
behaviors.
Here are the validation results. Xerxes
shows great fidelity. The idle latency
and bandwidth closely match the
hardware. The error rate is below 8%
with an average of just 4.3%.
Compared to existing emulation methods,
which deviate significantly under high
load, Xerxes remains accurate.
This accuracy holds across diverse
workloads and traffic patterns, unlike
simpler approaches that fall fail under
contention.
Finally, we show design space
exploration. Xerxes provides
architectural insights for
next-generation CXL systems. These
explorations uncover key design
considerations for scalable hardware.
We have several insights. The first
insight is about topology. As shown in
the charts, tree-like topologies suffer
from bottlenecks at the root switch. In
contrast, scalable topologies, like
spine-leaf, offer linear bandwidth
scaling because they provide multiple
paths.
The takeaway is that scalable topologies
are essential for high-performance CXL
fabrics. For example, tree topologies
lead to head-of-line blocking, while
spine-leaf distributes load, improving
overall system performance in
large-scale setups.
When simulating large-scale topology,
Xerxes is very efficient. It can
simulate up to 64 hosts in under 90
seconds,
using less than 200 MB of memory.
This makes it feasible to explore
large-scale topologies quickly.
The second insight focuses on device
managed coherence. We found that
hardware policies matter. For the victim
selection policy, LIFO, namely last in,
first out, works best. It reduces back
invalidations by about 16% by evicting
streaming data first. At the protocol
level, we found that an invalid block
length of two is the optimal sweet spot.
Specifically, LIFO is well suited for
the cache miss heavy patterns in snoop
filters, while the block length balances
performance benefits against bus
contention.
This demonstrates how Xerxes uniquely
facilitates the co-design of hardware
policies and protocol features.
The third insight highlights the
physical layer.
Full duplex transmission boost
bandwidth. With the 1:1 read-write mix,
you can approach twice the theoretical
bandwidth.
However, header overhead is a
constraint. Small packets with large
headers will diminish this gain. Xerxes
accurately models these physical layer
details.
This phenomenon arises from PCIe's
bidirectional links. Mixed workloads
maximize utilization, unlike single-type
accesses.
To summarize, Xerxes is the first
open-source simulator for CXL 3. It
supports topology of wire fabrics and
device managed coherence.
It is validated against hardware with an
average below 8%. The code is available
on GitHub.
Thank you for your attention. If you
have any questions, please contact the
original authors. Thank you.
